extracted.intended_audience: parliamentarians, legislative staff, policymakers, legal researchers, and civil-society stakeholders interested in India's law-making process
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and recommendations for improving the quality of Union government legislation in India, focusing on pre-legislative consultation, parliamentary committee scrutiny, and post‑legislative evaluation to reduce drafting defects and unintended consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-legislative stakeholder consultation
rubrics_metrics.description: Before bringing a bill to Parliament, the government should consult all stakeholders. It should put a draft out for public comments and use these inputs for strengthening its proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to push ministries to use public feedback to address stakeholder concerns and build consensus for smoother legislative journey and stronger laws. Anti-pattern: most bills are introduced without prior consultation (227 of 301 introduced without consultation since policy); consultation in India is non-binding so ministries often skip it. Example of good practice: labour ministry publishing the Social Security Code draft and revising it based on comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-legislative consultation policy requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The pre-legislative consultation policy specifies that a draft bill be placed in the public domain for 30 days for comments and that the justification, financial implications, and estimation of its impact should accompany the draft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy also prescribes that the ministry publishes the comments received on the draft on its website. Scoring/implementation notes: many drafts placed in public domain did not adhere to the 30‑day deadline; the policy is not binding on ministries, which limits compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed scrutiny by parliamentary subject committees
rubrics_metrics.description: Every government bill that reaches the legislature should go through detailed scrutiny by a parliamentary subject committee. Only after that examination should legislators discuss and pass the bill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee scrutiny compensates for MPs not being experts in every subject and allows detailed consideration, expert testimony, and travel to gather public feedback. Example: GST amendment (2017) committee travelled, heard experts, took ~18 months. Anti-pattern: government pressure to avoid committee referral (e.g., 2020 farm bills not referred). Statistical note: only 25% of bills referred to committees in 2014–19 Lok Sabha versus higher rates earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory/technical committee scrutiny for complex or constitution-amending bills
rubrics_metrics.description: Bills with technical nuances or constitutional amendment bills should be mandatorily examined by parliamentary committees rather than only debated on the floor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When laws are passed by simply debating on the floor it indicates Parliament is shrinking from its responsibility. Example contrast: 2019 10% reservation constitutional amendment passed within days without committee scrutiny versus lengthy committee-led GST process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-legislative evaluation and periodic review
rubrics_metrics.description: After Parliament has approved a law, it should periodically assess its functioning to determine whether the law is working or requires changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should be institutionalised rather than ad hoc; it informs whether the framework has gaps or created unintended problems. Examples of mechanisms: sunset clauses (Australia/Canada), statutory review provisions in Europe, government-appointed expert committees (used for the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code). Anti-pattern: in India no single institution routinely reviews laws and post‑legislative scrutiny by Parliament is episodic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutionalised post-legislative scrutiny mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Create or strengthen institutions and mechanisms for routine review of laws (e.g., sunset clauses, mandated statutory reviews, CAG performance audits, active Law Commission).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CAG can conduct performance audits of implementation (example: Food Security Act audit), but its workload limits coverage. The Law Commission (when functional) reviews legal aspects but is currently not functional. Institutionalisation increases systematic review rather than ad hoc or ministry-initiated evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency in publication of drafts, impacts and comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft bills should be published with justification, financial implications and estimated impacts, and ministries should publish the comments received on their drafts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency enables informed public participation and accountability. Anti-pattern: ministries frequently fail to publish drafts in a timely manner or to publish received comments; the pre-legislative consultation policy envisages but does not enforce this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resourcing MPs with research staff and support
rubrics_metrics.description: MPs need more resources (staff, research assistance) to scrutinise proposed legislation effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One alternative to mandatory committee scrutiny is enabling MPs to hire research staff, but in India MPs do not have a budget for such teams. Providing resources would strengthen legislative scrutiny capacity and reduce over-reliance on executive control of legislative agenda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hasty drafting — clarity of purpose, gaps and ambiguities
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws should be as free from defects as possible: free from gaps, ambiguities, and unclear purpose so as to reduce litigation and ensure effective implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poorly drafted laws are ineffective, create litigation, inconvenience the public and government, and can persist on statute books for long periods. Quoted judicial concern: many legislations have 'a lot of gaps, lot of ambiguities' causing confusion and litigation. Examples of harm: Inter State Migrant Workmen Act failure and retrospective tax amendment leading to arbitration (Vodafone, Cairn).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use committee hearings to gather expert testimony and stakeholder feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliamentary committees should hear testimony from experts and gather stakeholder input (including travelling to stakeholders) as part of their scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such hearings deepen technical understanding and public legitimacy of legislation. Example: the GST amendment committee held expert testimony and travelled across the country to gather public feedback, contributing to an extensive debate before passage.
